title: Beat Weird Openings
transcript: Kitty writes, "I know how to sacrifice the rook, but I am still around 800 Elo. Can you tell me what I do wrong? I play the London Dragon Sicilian King's Indian, but I keep losing some games." This is the 11th of reviewing my followers' games every single day until I hit 100,000 followers. If you want me to review your game, all you have to do is follow me, leave a like, and comment your chess.com username. Well, Kitty, I am sure you know your openings pretty well, but here's the issue. The moment that your opponent goes into something that is not a standard opening, you're folding. I found a few examples. In this game, you're playing black, and your opponent goes for this pretty early on attack of your F pawn. Whenever there is a bishop looking at the F pawn, and the opponent is trying to attack it, 90% of times the easiest way to just block all problems is to play E6. Now, we are ready to play H6 on the next move and push the knight back, and you're actually just better from the opening. Instead, you played D5, and in principle, I don't mind this move, but the issue is why would you not be solid when your opponent is very clearly playing something that is not standard, and so most likely not very good. After pawn takes and knight takes, it seems like you're defending the knight with the queen, but it is very easy for white to add more pressure and now attack the F pawn, and there is no way for you to hold onto everything. And here is another example. You fell for a very typical early on trap, where black sacrifices a knight, but you have to ask yourself, why is black giving me a knight? Are they really just blundering in the very first few moves of the game? And well, as it turns out, no. This is a tactic. They're going to sacrifice the bishop to win your queen, and now the game is over. And you took the knight in just 2 seconds. You have to consider your opponent's resources and look at checks, captures, and all that. You need to acknowledge the fact that once you open up here, the queens are going to be seeing each other, and the fact that this bishop is able to deliver a check. And here is another example. You develop your pieces quite normally, and your opponent again is trying to attack the F pawn early on. By the way, I don't know why you would want to give up the G pawn. That is just a blunder, even without the attack on the F pawn. But on the next move, you don't do anything to acknowledge this attack. You have to look at what your opponent's pieces are trying to do. You have two pieces looking at this pawn, and a knight very advanced. So, you have to look at what the threats are. And you almost pre-move your next move. You play Bishop to H6 in 1 second. The opening is really no place to be pre-moving stuff. And so, on the next move, you hang this fork, and you just resigned the game. Now, I know that you don't lose every game like this, but this is a very big hole in your play. You have to be prepared against lines that you don't have the time to study, or there is no need to study, because they are just bad. For example, in this case, even after blundering the G pawn, you are fine after playing something like E6. Again, blocking this diagonal.
